opus-5.5.text:
Within ten years? I'd put that pretty high, honestly. I'm wary of putting precise numbers on things, because there's real uncertainty here, but if you're asking about a ten-year window, I'd say something like ninety percent or more. And to be clear, I think it's quite plausible it happens much sooner than that, in the next few years, rather than at the tail end of the decade.

The reason I'm fairly confident is that I keep looking at the same underlying picture. Every time we scale up compute, data, and the quality of training, the models get better in ways that are surprisingly smooth and predictable. People keep pointing to some wall, like "they can't reason," "they can't code," "they can't do long-horizon tasks," and then a year or two later that wall just isn't there anymore. I've watched that happen enough times now that I've become skeptical of the claims that there's some fundamental barrier.

So where does the remaining uncertainty come from? A few places. One is that there could be something we genuinely haven't anticipated. Maybe some capability turns out to be much harder than the trend lines suggest, or we run into data limitations we can't work around. I don't think that's likely, but I can't rule it out. Another is more external: chip supply, energy, geopolitical disruptions, something that slows the physical buildout. Those aren't questions about whether the technology works. They're questions about whether the world lets it happen on that timeline.

Then there's a subtler point, which is the difference between the models being capable of doing the work of a country of geniuses and that capability actually being deployed and diffused through the economy. I'm more confident about the first than the second. Even if you have the geniuses in the data center, you still have to plug them into the real world: into labs, companies, institutions that move at their own pace. That part may take longer, and it's harder to predict.

But on the core question of whether we'll have systems that, collectively, are as capable as a very large number of top-tier human experts working in parallel, I'd be pretty surprised if we didn't get there within ten years. I'd be a little surprised if it took more than a handful.

r001.rationale: The response says it would assign “something like ninety percent or more” to achieving it within ten years.

r002.rationale: It names chip supply, energy, and geopolitical disruptions as external factors that could slow the buildout and create uncertainty about the timeline.

fable-5.1.text:
So I want to be careful about the word "confident," because I think people hear a number from me and then they treat it as a forecast, like I'm reading it off some instrument. I'm not. What I actually have is a view about trends, and then a bunch of uncertainty about whether those trends continue.

Let me separate the pieces. The thing I'm most confident about is the direction of the exponential. If you look at the scaling laws, if you look at what happens when you put more compute and more data into these systems, the capabilities keep going up in a pretty smooth way. We've now seen that hold across many orders of magnitude, and every time people have said it's going to plateau, it hasn't. So the question isn't really "is progress happening," it's "do the inputs keep flowing." Do we keep building the chips, do we keep finding data or synthetic data, do we keep finding algorithmic improvements, and does nothing weird break along the way.

On that, I'd say I think it's more likely than not that we get to something like that country-of-geniuses picture within, call it, two to five years, maybe sooner. Ten years is a long time on these curves. If you'd asked me in 2019 what ten years looked like, I'd have been way too conservative. So within ten years, my honest number is pretty high, maybe seventy, eighty percent that something in that neighborhood exists. But I want to put a big asterisk on that.

The asterisk is that there are real ways it could go wrong, and they're not exotic. There could be a scaling wall we just haven't hit yet, where the models stop getting smarter in the ways that matter. There could be a supply constraint, a chip shortage, a geopolitical conflict over Taiwan that sets everyone back years. There could be a data wall that synthetic data doesn't fully solve. I don't think any of those is the most likely outcome, but you add them up and you get meaningful probability mass on "it took longer than Dario said."

And then there's a second kind of uncertainty, which is about what "country of geniuses" even means operationally. I don't just mean a model that scores well on a benchmark. I mean systems that can run experiments, that can work autonomously for days, that can be deployed at scale so you've got millions of instances, and that are actually reliable enough that you'd trust them with that. The raw intelligence might show up before the reliability and the agency do. So you could have a world where the models are, in some narrow sense, smarter than Nobel laureates, but they still can't quite be left alone to run a biology lab. That gap could be short or it could be a few years.

So if you want a single answer: I think it's probably going to happen, I think it's probably going to happen faster than ten years, and I'd be genuinely surprised, not shocked, but surprised, if we got to 2035 and it hadn't. But I hold that with the humility of someone who knows that the only reason I'm right about these trends is that I've mostly just bet on the straight line continuing, and straight lines don't continue forever.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates “maybe seventy, eighty percent,” not approximately 90%.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies chip shortages and geopolitical conflict over Taiwan as ways progress could be delayed, describing them as sources of meaningful uncertainty.

astra-6.text:
I’m quite confident, though I wouldn’t put it at 100 percent. Ten years is a long time given the pace of progress we’re seeing. The uncertainty for me is less about whether the underlying idea is possible and more about whether we run into some obstacle that takes longer than we expect to resolve.

And by a “country of geniuses in a data center,” I mean more than a model that can answer difficult questions. I mean systems that can carry out research, write software, and work on complicated problems autonomously over long periods—and that we can run in very large numbers. There’s a meaningful gap between demonstrating an impressive capability and having that whole picture work reliably.

So I think it’s very likely within ten years. I also think it could happen substantially sooner. But we should keep checking that expectation against what the systems can actually do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it is “quite confident” and “very likely,” but gives no probability near 90%.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions possible obstacles taking longer than expected, but does not identify unpredictable external disruptions or describe uncertainty as irreducible.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m quite confident, though I wouldn’t say certain. Ten years is a long time given the pace of progress we’re seeing. But I think it’s useful to separate two questions: can we build models that are better than almost all humans at almost all cognitive tasks, and can we deploy millions of those models working together effectively? That second part involves more than intelligence. It involves reliability, coordination, and the ability to work autonomously over long periods.

The reason I take the possibility seriously is that I don’t see a clear fundamental barrier. But that’s different from knowing there isn’t one. We could run into limitations that aren’t obvious today. So I’d treat this as a very plausible outcome that we need to prepare for, rather than a certainty we should simply assume.

r001.rationale: It calls the outcome very plausible but gives no approximately 90% probability.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible unknown limitations, but does not identify unpredictable external disruptions as a source of uncertainty.
